segments.speaker: John
segments.text: In Deep Reinforcement Learning Methods, today’s lecture is on Diffusion Reward Models. Recent work such as Energy-Based Reward Models for Robust Language Model Alignment and Probabilistic Uncertain Reward Model reflects a broader move toward representing complex preferences more carefully. This paper, from a team led at Tsinghua University with collaborators at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, asks whether rewards should be distributions rather than single scores. That matters when human judgments conflict. Yes, Noah?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hi Professor, if reward models already rank responses, why do we need a whole distribution?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Because a ranking or scalar score hides how much evaluators disagree. The paper argues that the same response can reasonably receive different judgments, perhaps because annotators weigh helpfulness, correctness, and safety differently. Diffusion Reward Models learn a conditional distribution of rewards for each prompt and response. Think of a single score as a class average; the distribution also tells us whether the class agreed or split into distinct groups.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Quick question: does predicting several attributes already capture that disagreement?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Not necessarily. A multi-attribute model can predict helpfulness, safety, and other predefined dimensions, but it still often summarizes each dimension with one value. This paper’s multi-attribute version predicts 19 reward dimensions, while also modeling a distribution over possible reward values. That distinction matters: the attributes describe what is being judged, while the distribution captures variation in how those judgments may be made.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The architecture separates language understanding from reward generation. A frozen 8-billion-parameter language encoder processes the prompt and response, and its final-token representation is stored for later use. A much smaller Diffusion Transformer reward head then learns to generate rewards conditioned on that representation. The head has about 12 million trainable parameters, so the language encoder remains fixed while the reward distribution is learned.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Can you clarify how the model learns from datasets that label different attributes?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: For multi-attribute training, a mask excludes missing labels from the denoising loss, so datasets with different attribute coverage can contribute without pretending every example has every annotation. For pairwise preferences, the authors create centered pseudo-rewards and add a Bradley-Terry ranking loss. That encourages the preferred response to score above the rejected one. The authors also note that this is a practical surrogate, not an exact comparison of the full reward distributions.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: At inference, the reward head starts with Gaussian noise and uses D-D-I-M reverse diffusion to produce multiple reward samples for one response. The default uses 10 steps and 32 samples, with a guidance scale of 7. Their mean gives a conventional score; variation across samples estimates uncertainty. More samples can stabilize the estimate without requiring more candidate responses, though repeated sampling adds computation.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Does that extra computation make the method impractical for ranking many responses?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: It is a real trade-off, but the reported default inference cost is about 1.63 times that of the scalar baseline, with samples processed in parallel. The authors also use uncertainty for selective prediction: systems can abstain on ambiguous cases and send them for review. In tests, rejecting the most uncertain examples improved retained accuracy, including an average gain of 2.81 percentage points at 70% coverage on a correctness benchmark.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The distributions also appear to track actual disagreement. On repeated human ratings, diffusion samples better matched empirical helpfulness ratings than point estimates and simple global distribution baselines across several distance measures. The model produced multimodal outputs more often when people disagreed strongly: the multimodal rate rose from 37.6% on low-range examples to 63.2% on polarized ones. This suggests the model can preserve structure that a mean would erase.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So does a higher average reward still make the best response?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Not always. For risk-sensitive selection, the authors score responses using the mean minus 0.4 times the standard deviation, favoring high rewards that are also relatively stable. This improved best-of-candidate results over mean-only selection, though gains were generally under one percentage point. In downstream reinforcement learning from human feedback, policies trained with this reward model also outperformed the reported scalar baselines on Arena-Hard v2 and MT-Bench.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The benchmark results show a useful but qualified improvement. The multi-attribute diffusion model averaged 66.2, compared with 62.3 for its matched scalar baseline and 64.1 for a quantile-based model. The pairwise-trained version averaged 65.8. Their strengths differ: multi-attribute training did better on correctness-oriented tasks, while pairwise training did slightly better on preference-oriented ones. The largest models in the comparison still scored higher overall.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How does this differ from the probabilistic reward-model work you mentioned at the start?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The shared motivation is to move beyond a single certain-looking score. The distinction here is the modeling mechanism: diffusion can represent flexible, potentially multimodal reward distributions without choosing a fixed Gaussian or quantile grid in advance. That complements work on energy-based and probabilistic reward models rather than replacing it. The results also suggest that richer reward representations can support abstention and risk-aware selection, not just improve a benchmark average.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: What should we be cautious about before applying it in a safety-critical system?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The evidence is promising but bounded. Experiments use one frozen 8-billion-parameter encoder and a few hundred thousand training examples, so scaling to other model families and much larger data remains untested. The pairwise objective approximates distribution-level preference learning, and repeated sampling costs more than scalar scoring. Nor does uncertainty remove biases inherited from annotation data. Before deployment, we would need broader evaluations, especially on harmful or persuasive-but-false responses.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The central takeaway is that a reward need not be a verdict carved in stone. It can be a distribution that records both expected preference and uncertainty about that preference. Diffusion Reward Models offer one way to learn and use that richer signal, with practical costs and open questions still in view. For alignment research, the important next step is testing when disagreement-aware rewards lead to safer decisions, rather than assuming that a more detailed score is automatically better.
